tagline: From an abolitionist village to the Ohio River.
intro: From Mount Pleasant, the byway runs down to Rayland on the Ohio River. Antislavery Quakers laid out Mount Pleasant in 1803 around Union and Concord streets, and the plan is still intact. The village became a well-known haven on the Underground Railroad.

Charles Osborn began The Philanthropist here in 1817, the first newspaper in the country to call for abolition, and Benjamin Lundy's Genius of Universal Emancipation followed a few years later. The Quakers' 1814 meetinghouse held the first yearly meeting west of the Alleghenies. After the Civil War, the railroads passed the village by.

moments.title: Benjamin Lundy House
moments.text: Lundy lived a year in this brick house, which served the Underground Railroad and held one of the few known free produce stores, selling nothing made by enslaved labor.

moments.title: Connorville
moments.text: Route 150 runs along the south side of this Short Creek valley community, where a coal mine once employed 60 men.

moments.title: Rayland
moments.text: Called Portland Station until 1928, the village was in its heyday among the larger port towns on the Ohio River.
